references.text: Jesus says in the Sermon on the Mount that if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even tax collectors do the same? The same principle applies: goodness shown only to those who are good to you deserves no reward.
The context of Luke 6:33 — Jesus encourages doing good to enemies, not just to those who do good to us.
The preceding verse raises the parallel question about loving those who love you, with the same conclusion: even sinners do that.
The following verse continues the same pattern by lending to those from whom you expect repayment, and concludes with an encouragement to do good without expecting anything in return.
Peter brings up the same principle: What credit is it if you endure when you sin and are beaten? But if you endure when you do good and suffer, that is a grace from God.

Jesus encourages loving enemies and praying for persecutors, so that you may be children of your heavenly Father who causes the sun to rise on both evil and good — a parallel to the principle of doing good beyond what is expected.
Proverbs teach to do good to one's enemy — give him food and drink — which goes beyond merely doing good to those who do good to you.
Paul quotes Proverbs and encourages overcoming evil with good, which is the same principle Jesus conveys in Luke 6:33.
